questions.question_text: Checks and balances ensure that:
questions.option_b: each branch can limit the powers of the others
questions.explanation: Checks and balances let each branch restrain the others (veto, judicial review, confirmation), preventing any one from dominating. It complements separation of powers.

questions.question_text: The elastic clause (Necessary and Proper Clause) gives Congress the power to:
questions.option_b: make laws needed to carry out its enumerated powers
questions.explanation: The elastic clause lets Congress pass laws 'necessary and proper' to execute its listed powers, the basis for implied powers (upheld in McCulloch v. Maryland). It expands federal authority.

questions.question_text: Anti-Federalists' demand for a Bill of Rights reflected their fear of:
questions.option_b: a strong central government threatening individual liberties
questions.explanation: Anti-Federalists worried a powerful national government would trample rights, so they insisted on explicit protections—producing the Bill of Rights. This debate shaped ratification.

questions.question_text: The President serves as Commander-in-Chief of the:
questions.option_b: armed forces
questions.explanation: Article II makes the president Commander-in-Chief of the military, though Congress holds the power to declare war and fund it—a key separation of war powers.

questions.question_text: Impeachment of a federal official begins in the House and is tried in the:
questions.option_b: Senate
questions.explanation: The House impeaches (charges) by majority; the Senate tries the case, needing 2/3 to convict and remove. Separating accusation and trial across chambers is a deliberate check.

questions.question_text: An appropriations bill is legislation that:
questions.option_b: authorizes the spending of government funds
questions.explanation: Appropriations bills fund government operations, giving Congress its 'power of the purse.' Failure to pass them can cause government shutdowns—a major point of legislative leverage.

questions.question_text: A standing committee in Congress is:
questions.option_b: a permanent committee specializing in a policy area that handles most legislation
questions.explanation: Standing committees (Judiciary, Armed Services) are permanent and do the detailed work of reviewing bills in their domain. They are where most legislation lives or dies.

questions.question_text: The Fifth Amendment protects against:
questions.option_b: self-incrimination and double jeopardy, and guarantees due process
questions.explanation: The Fifth Amendment includes the right against self-incrimination ('plead the Fifth'), protection from double jeopardy, and due process. Other protections belong to different amendments.

questions.question_text: Selective incorporation means that:
questions.option_a: all rights apply to states at once
questions.option_b: the Supreme Court applies Bill of Rights protections to states one at a time via the 14th Amendment
questions.option_c: states ignore the Bill of Rights
questions.explanation: Through selective incorporation, the Court has extended most Bill of Rights protections to the states case by case using the 14th Amendment's due process clause. It's a gradual, case-driven process.

questions.question_text: McDonald v. Chicago (2010) is significant because it:
questions.option_b: incorporated the Second Amendment, applying it to state and local governments
questions.explanation: McDonald used the 14th Amendment to incorporate the Second Amendment, so states must respect the individual right to bear arms affirmed in Heller. It extended a federal right to the states.

questions.question_text: A scientific opinion poll seeks to be representative by using:
questions.option_b: a random sample of the population
questions.explanation: Random sampling gives every member an equal chance of selection, producing representative, generalizable results. Non-random samples introduce bias and can't be reliably projected to the population.

questions.question_text: The family is generally considered the most important agent of:
questions.option_b: political socialization
questions.explanation: Family is typically the earliest and strongest influence on political values and party identification. Other agents (school, media, peers) build on this foundation.

questions.question_text: A 'liberal' position on the role of government in the economy typically favors:
questions.option_b: more government intervention to reduce inequality and regulate markets
questions.explanation: On economics, U.S. liberals favor active government—regulation, social programs, progressive taxation—to address inequality. Conservatives generally favor limited intervention and free markets.

questions.question_text: The 26th Amendment lowered the voting age to:
questions.explanation: The 26th Amendment (1971) set the voting age at 18, partly responding to the argument that those drafted for Vietnam should be able to vote. It expanded suffrage to young adults.

questions.question_text: Interest groups differ from political parties in that interest groups:
questions.option_a: run candidates for office under their own label
questions.option_b: seek to influence policy without nominating their own candidates
questions.explanation: Interest groups lobby and advocate on specific issues but don't field candidates as parties do. Parties aim to win elections and govern broadly; groups pursue narrower policy goals.

questions.question_text: The 'electoral college' allocates each state a number of electors equal to:
questions.option_b: its total number of senators plus representatives
questions.explanation: Each state gets electors equal to its House seats plus two senators (DC gets 3), totaling 538. This blends population (House) with equal state representation (Senate).

questions.question_text: A confederation is a system in which:
questions.option_a: the national government holds most power
questions.option_b: independent states retain most power and the central government is weak
questions.explanation: In a confederation, sovereign states delegate limited powers to a weak central authority (as under the Articles). Its weaknesses motivated the shift to a stronger federal system.

questions.question_text: The federal bureaucracy primarily functions to:
questions.option_b: implement and enforce laws passed by Congress
questions.explanation: Agencies carry out laws through rulemaking and enforcement, exercising discretionary authority Congress delegates. The bureaucracy is the executive branch's machinery for governing.

questions.question_text: The 'clear and present danger' test (Schenck) was later refined by Brandenburg v. Ohio to protect speech unless it incites:
questions.option_b: imminent lawless action
questions.explanation: Brandenburg narrowed restrictions: speech is protected unless it's directed to and likely to incite imminent lawless action. This raised the bar for limiting expression.

questions.question_text: Public opinion is most accurately measured by:
questions.option_b: scientific random-sample polling with a stated margin of error
questions.explanation: Random-sample polls with reported margins of error yield reliable, generalizable measures of opinion. Self-selected online polls and anecdotes are biased and unrepresentative.

questions.question_text: A super PAC differs from a traditional PAC in that a super PAC can:
questions.option_a: donate unlimited money directly to candidates
questions.option_b: raise and spend unlimited money on independent expenditures, but not coordinate with campaigns
questions.explanation: Super PACs (post-Citizens United) make unlimited independent expenditures but can't coordinate with or donate directly to candidates. Traditional PACs face contribution limits but can give to campaigns.

questions.question_text: The federal court system's highest court is the:
questions.option_b: Supreme Court
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court is the highest federal court, with nine justices and final say on constitutional questions. Below it sit the Courts of Appeals and District Courts.

questions.question_text: Federalist No. 70 argues for:
questions.option_b: a single energetic executive for accountability and effective leadership
questions.explanation: Hamilton's Federalist 70 defends a single, vigorous executive as essential for decisive action and clear accountability. It's a foundational argument for presidential power (though not a required AP document, it illustrates the debate).

questions.question_text: The First Amendment protects freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly, and:
questions.option_b: the right to petition the government
questions.explanation: The First Amendment's five freedoms are religion, speech, press, assembly, and petition. The other options belong to different amendments (Second, Sixth, Fourth).

questions.question_text: An exit poll surveys voters:
questions.option_b: as they leave polling places, to project results and analyze voting patterns
questions.explanation: Exit polls question voters right after voting, helping media project winners and understand demographic patterns. They can be inaccurate, so analysts use them cautiously.

questions.question_text: Voter turnout is generally highest in:
questions.option_b: presidential elections
questions.explanation: Presidential elections draw the most voters due to high stakes and media attention; midterms, primaries, and local races see lower turnout. Salience drives participation.

questions.question_text: A pocket veto occurs when the president:
questions.option_b: takes no action on a bill and Congress adjourns within 10 days, killing it
questions.explanation: If the president neither signs nor returns a bill within 10 days and Congress adjourns, the bill dies via pocket veto—which Congress cannot override. It's a quiet form of rejection.

questions.question_text: Grants-in-aid (federal funds to states) are a tool of:
questions.option_b: fiscal federalism, used to influence state policy
questions.explanation: Through grants (categorical and block), the federal government funds and steers state policy—fiscal federalism. Conditions attached to grants extend federal influence into state matters.
